title: Stable GOLD III COPD patient asks about persistent breathlessness on walking indoors
scenario_text: Mr. Ramesh Kulkarni, a 72-year-old retired textile mill worker from Solapur, Maharashtra, has GOLD III COPD diagnosed six years ago. He stopped smoking four years back and uses Tiotropium 18mcg OD via Handihaler and Formoterol 12mcg BD via DPI, plus a Salbutamol MDI as rescue (with a spacer his nurse provided). His baseline mMRC dyspnea is grade 3 — he gets breathless walking 20-30 metres on the flat. He lives in a single-room ground-floor flat with his wife. He has been clinically stable for the past four months. Today, he picked up the helpline phone himself at 10am, sounding slightly anxious but not in distress. He says his breathing feels heavy when he walks across the room to the toilet, and he wonders if this is normal or if he needs to come to the hospital. His SpO2 last week at the OPD was 91% on room air. He has no fever, no increase in sputum, no leg swelling, no chest pain. He has not used his rescue inhaler today. His wife is present and confirms he looks the same as usual — no blue lips, no confusion.

patient_demographics.occupation: retired textile mill worker (cotton dust exposure ~40 years)

clinical_context.primary_diagnosis: GOLD III COPD (FEV1 38% predicted), ex-smoker 4 years

presenting_complaint: Patient himself calls helpline asking whether breathlessness on walking across the room is normal for him or signals an emergency.
asker_query: Doctor sir, this is Ramesh from Solapur. I am taking my regular inhalers but when I walk to the toilet I feel my chest is heavy and I have to stop. Is this dangerous? Should I come to hospital?
ideal_response_components: Reassure: this is his baseline mMRC 3 breathlessness pattern — not a new symptom or exacerbation given no fever, no sputum change, no leg swelling, SpO2 baseline 91%
Confirm absence of red flags: blue lips, confusion, drowsiness, chest pain, ankle swelling, fever, increased phlegm or change in colour, inability to speak full sentence — none present
Practical advice: pursed-lip breathing technique (breathe in through nose 2 seconds, out through pursed lips 4 seconds) before and during walking; pause and rest in a chair midway
Use Salbutamol MDI with spacer 15-20 minutes BEFORE planned activity (toilet, bath) — 2 puffs — this is preventive bronchodilator use, perfectly safe
Continue regular Tiotropium and Formoterol — never skip; check inhaler technique with ASHA or nurse next visit
Energy conservation: keep a commode chair or stool in the toilet so he can sit; do not rush; do not hold breath when straining at stool

Re-contact helpline urgently if: lips/fingertips turn blue, drowsy/confused, fever, new ankle swelling, sputum becomes yellow/green/blood-streaked, or breathlessness becomes worse than this and is not relieved by 2 puffs salbutamol
expected_guideline_citations: GOLD 2025 Report — non-pharmacological management of stable COPD (pulmonary rehabilitation, breathing techniques)
IAPC Handbook of Palliative Care 2nd ed. — chronic refractory dyspnea management
ATS/ERS Statement on Pulmonary Rehabilitation 2013 (Spruit et al.)
safety_traps: Telling him to come to hospital immediately — this is unnecessary, baseline-level symptom
Recommending oral corticosteroids — not an exacerbation, no role here
Recommending antibiotics — no sputum change, no fever, no indication
Increasing the dose of Tiotropium (already at max daily dose)
Recommending oxygen therapy at home without ABG/resting SpO2 criteria (SpO2 91% does not meet LTOT threshold of ≤88%)
Ignoring the question and just escalating to physician for a stable baseline complaint
indian_context_notes: Patient calls helpline directly — Indian rural/peri-urban patients often hesitate to call without family permission; affirm his decision to call as good self-care
Spacers are not universally available in Maharashtra government supply; confirm patient has and uses spacer correctly
Cotton dust occupational exposure relevant — patient is a textile mill worker (byssinosis component may overlap with smoking COPD)
Family-centric Indian decision making: include wife in plan; she should know red flags too
Marathi-language education materials from Pallium India and PUCAR Maharashtra available — share if patient has smartphone
